html:
Introduction

Starting a Hospice in Maryland represents a meaningful opportunity to serve individuals with terminal illnesses requiring end-of-life care while building a compliant, sustainable care business. This is a deeply rewarding field that provides comfort, dignity, and support to patients and their families during one of life’s most challenging phases. Oversight and funding are administered by the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) Office of Health Care Quality (OHCQ), which is the primary state licensing body. Reimbursement and program funding are coordinated through Maryland Medicaid and the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).

With significant workforce shortages and access limitations, particularly in rural areas, and reimbursement rates including a Medicaid per diem of $160-$190 and a Medicare per diem around $200 for routine home care, Maryland offers a competitive but opportunity-rich market for providers prepared to navigate its unique regulatory landscape. The state’s most significant hurdle and, simultaneously, a barrier to market saturation is the requirement for a Certificate of Need (CON), which ensures that new services meet a demonstrated community need.

This comprehensive guide walks you through every step of launching a Hospice in Maryland, from understanding the complex regulations and the critical CON process to staffing your interdisciplinary team, managing reimbursement, and preparing for state and federal inspections. Whether you are an experienced healthcare professional or an entrepreneur with a passion for compassionate care, this roadmap will provide the clarity needed to succeed.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Maryland’s Hospice Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Maryland’s Hospice Regulations

Navigating the regulatory environment is the first and most critical step in your journey. Maryland regulates Hospice programs through the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) Office of Health Care Quality (OHCQ). This agency is responsible for overseeing licensure and requiring a Certificate of Need (CON) approval, ensuring new services meet a demonstrated community need. The CON process is a formal review that prevents the over-saturation of healthcare services and is a major component of the Maryland hospice license application process.

Providers serving Medicaid or federally funded populations, which includes virtually all hospices, must also comply with federal frameworks, most notably the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Conditions of Participation (CoPs) and the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). The CMS CoPs are the foundational rules for quality and operational integrity, and achieving Medicare certification is essential for financial viability. The regulatory framework in Maryland emphasizes a strong focus on meeting demonstrated community need (via the CON process), quality of care, patient rights, and comprehensive care planning. Licenses are granted after a rigorous review and typically require renewal every 2 years, contingent on successful surveys and continued compliance.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

While the core hospice license is singular, Maryland’s market dynamics support multiple service specializations, each with different clinical, staffing, and marketing considerations. Focusing on a niche can differentiate your agency and address specific community needs, which can also strengthen your CON application.

  • General Hospice Care: This is the foundation of most agencies, providing the four required levels of care (Routine Home Care, Continuous Care, Inpatient Respite Care, and General Inpatient Care) for the adult and geriatric population.
  • Pediatric Hospice: A highly specialized niche providing end-of-life care for children, adolescents, and their families. This requires staff with specific pediatric palliative expertise and different psychosocial support models.
  • Culturally Competent Hospice: Designing services tailored to the specific cultural, linguistic, and spiritual needs of Maryland’s diverse communities. This can be a powerful differentiator in urban areas like Baltimore and the D.C. suburbs.
  • Palliative Care Integration: While distinct from hospice, many agencies are offering palliative care services to patients with serious chronic illnesses earlier in their disease trajectory. This can serve as a natural bridge to hospice care when the time is right.

Program size is measured by Average Daily Census (ADC), not physical beds (unless you operate an inpatient unit). A new agency might start by targeting an ADC of 20-50 patients. Demand is strongest in the densely populated Baltimore and Washington D.C. metropolitan areas. However, these regions also have the most competition. In contrast, rural areas of Maryland have sparse availability and may offer significant entry opportunities with less competition, a factor the CON commission may view favorably.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Before you can apply for a license, you must establish a formal business entity. In Maryland, providers typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or a Corporation (S-Corp or C-Corp). Each structure has different implications for liability, taxation, and governance, so consulting with a legal and financial advisor is crucial.

Once your business entity is formed, you must complete several foundational steps:

  • Register your business with the Maryland Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (malpractice), and workers’ compensation.
  • Begin the Certificate of Need (CON) process with the Maryland Health Care Commission (MHCC), which precedes the license application.
  • Submit a licensing application to the MDH Office of Health Care Quality (OHCQ) after receiving CON approval.

Be prepared for a lengthy timeline. The entire process, from starting the CON application to achieving full licensure and Medicare certification, generally ranges from 12 to 24 months. The completeness of your application, the strength of your CON argument, and your readiness for the initial licensing survey will all impact this timeline.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is not just a document for lenders; it’s your operational blueprint. It must detail your financial projections, market strategy, and path to profitability. Startup costs for a hospice in Maryland typically range from $150,000 to $400,000. This covers CON and licensing fees, legal and consulting expenses, initial staff salaries, office setup, electronic medical record (EMR) software, and at least six months of operating runway.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by your interdisciplinary team. Staffing represents 60-70% of total costs, a standard benchmark in healthcare services. Your financial model must be built around projected reimbursement rates. A typical revenue snapshot includes:

  • Maryland Medicaid Routine Home Care: $160 – $190 per diem
  • Medicare Routine Home Care: Approximately $200 per diem
  • Higher Levels of Care: Rates for Continuous Care, General Inpatient Care, and Inpatient Respite Care are significantly higher and are billed on an hourly or daily basis, respectively.

Profitability depends on managing your census and controlling costs. The break-even point for a new hospice is often 12-18 months post-launch. Providers who successfully manage their operations and achieve a sustainable Average Daily Census (ADC) based on staffing levels can generally achieve gross 10-15% margins.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

While most hospice care is delivered in the patient’s home, your agency requires a physical administrative office. This office is the hub for your clinical teams, administrative staff, and record-keeping. Your facility must meet specific requirements:

  • An administrative office that is accessible to staff and, if necessary, the public, and complies with local zoning ordinances.
  • Secure, locked storage for physical patient records and a secure IT infrastructure for electronic records to ensure HIPAA compliance.
  • A dedicated, private space for the interdisciplinary team to hold meetings and discuss patient care.
  • Adequate space for supplies, equipment, and administrative functions.

If you plan to offer General Inpatient (GIP) or respite care directly, you will need to either build or contract with a facility that meets stringent state and federal health and safety codes for inpatient care. Location selection for your office should consider proximity to major referral sources like hospitals, accessibility for your staff covering the service area, and the availability of a qualified clinical workforce.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your staff is the heart of your hospice. The quality of your care is a direct reflection of the team you build. CMS and Maryland regulations mandate a core Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) that develops and reviews every patient’s plan of care. Required roles typically include:

  • Medical Director: A physician (MD or DO) who provides clinical oversight and direction for the hospice team.
  • Administrator / Director of Patient Services: A Registered Nurse (RN) responsible for the day-to-day operations and clinical management of the agency.
  • Registered Nurses (RN Case Managers): Lead the coordination and provision of direct patient care.
  • Social Workers (MSW): Address the psychosocial needs of the patient and family.
  • Spiritual Counselors / Chaplains: Provide spiritual support aligned with the patient’s and family’s beliefs.
  • Bereavement Coordinator: Manages the bereavement support program for families for up to 13 months after the patient’s death.
  • Hospice Aides (CNA/HHA): Provide personal care to the patient under the supervision of an RN.
  • Volunteer Coordinator: Recruits, trains, and manages volunteers, whose service hours must equal at least 5% of total patient care hours.

All staff must undergo comprehensive training. Required training includes initial orientation on the hospice philosophy, pain and symptom management, patient rights, safety protocols, and emergency procedures. Additionally, ongoing annual continuing education is mandated in areas like infection control, compliance, and clinical best practices to meet Maryland hospice requirements.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Comprehensive, well-documented policies and procedures are the backbone of a compliant hospice agency. They are your rulebook for operations and will be scrutinized during your initial licensing survey and subsequent inspections. Maryland and CMS require written policies covering all aspects of your operation, including:

  • Patient Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria
  • Plan of Care Development, Review, and Update Processes
  • Pain and Symptom Management Protocols
  • Patient Rights and Grievance Procedures
  • Emergency Preparedness Plan
  • Infection Control and Prevention
  • Staffing, Supervision, and Volunteer Management
  • Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI) Program

Individualized care plans are central to hospice. The IDG must develop a detailed, patient-specific plan of care within 48 hours of admission. This plan must be regularly reviewed and updated based on the patient’s changing needs and goals. Meticulous documentation of these plans and the IDG meetings where they are discussed is a frequent focus of surveyors.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Hospice marketing is not about direct-to-consumer advertising; it is about building trust and strong relationships within the local healthcare community. Your referrals will come from professionals who trust your agency to provide timely, compassionate, and reliable care. Key referral sources include:

  • Hospital Discharge Planners and Case Managers
  • Oncologists, Cardiologists, and other Specialist Physicians
  • Skilled Nursing Facilities (SNFs)
  • Assisted Living Facilities
  • Home Health Agencies
  • Primary Care Physicians

Successful providers focus on demonstrating compliance, being highly responsive to referral requests, and providing excellent clinical outcomes and communication. Your marketing efforts should be led by a clinical liaison or marketer who can educate these sources on your services, admission criteria, and unique value proposition (e.g., pediatric or culturally-specific programs). Building these relationships takes time and consistency and should begin long before you are ready to admit your first patient.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Achieving licensure is the beginning, not the end, of your compliance journey. Your agency will be subject to ongoing oversight from both state and federal bodies. Oversight includes unannounced surveys from the MDH Office of Health Care Quality (OHCQ) and CMS (or its deemed accreditation organizations like CHAP or ACHC). These inspections are rigorous and focus on ensuring you are adhering to your own policies and all regulatory standards.

Common deficiencies found during hospice surveys often relate to documentation and process failures. These include:

  • Incomplete or outdated Plans of Care
  • Lack of thorough documentation for Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) meetings
  • Medication management and reconciliation errors
  • Insufficient documentation of hospice aide supervision by an RN
  • Failure to provide or document required bereavement support services

A proactive approach is essential. Implement a robust Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI) program to continuously monitor your own performance, identify potential issues, and correct them before a surveyor finds them. Maintaining audit-ready documentation at all times is not just a best practice—it is a condition of survival.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How long does it take to open a Hospice in Maryland?

A: Due to the mandatory Certificate of Need (CON) process, the timeline is longer than in many other states. You should expect the entire process, from starting your business entity to achieving full licensure and Medicare certification, to take 12 to 24 months.

Q: What licenses are required to start a hospice in Maryland?

A: You must first obtain a Certificate of Need (CON) from the Maryland Health Care Commission. With an approved CON, you can then apply for a state hospice license from the MDH Office of Health Care Quality (OHCQ). Finally, you must achieve Medicare and Maryland Medicaid certification to be eligible for reimbursement.

Q: What reimbursement is available for hospice services in Maryland?

A: Reimbursement is primarily available through Medicare and Maryland Medicaid on a per diem (per day) basis. The rates vary by the level of care provided. For Routine Home Care, you can expect approximately $200/day from Medicare and $160-$190/day from Maryland Medicaid. Higher rates apply for Continuous Care, General Inpatient Care, and Inpatient Respite Care.

Conclusion

Starting a hospice in Maryland is a complex but profoundly impactful endeavor. The state’s regulatory environment, particularly the Certificate of Need requirement, demands careful planning, significant upfront investment, and unwavering attention to detail. However, the clear need for more services, especially in rural areas and for specialized populations, presents a real opportunity for dedicated providers.

Providers who invest in a deep understanding of the regulations, build a compassionate and qualified team, and cultivate strong referral relationships are positioned for long-term success and sustainability. By prioritizing compliance, quality care, and operational discipline from day one, you can build a hospice agency that not only thrives as a business but also serves as a vital resource for your community.
